title: Designing Reliable Tools
learning_outcomes: Explain single-purpose tool design and how it connects to designing reliable tools.
Apply clear descriptions and typed arguments in the example and predict the output before running it.
Test one realistic edge case for designing reliable tools and explain what the example does not prove.

content.intro: This lesson covers designing reliable tools through 6 syllabus subtopics preserved from the supplied Generative AI curriculum. Use schema-constrained outputs and tool calls as a controlled application protocol. A model request is a proposal, not proof that an external action is authorized or completed.
content.why_it_matters: Single-purpose tool design describes one part of a controlled action loop. The model may propose a step, but the application should independently validate the arguments, check the caller's permissions, enforce step/time limits, and record the actual tool result before deciding what happens next.

items.title: Clear descriptions and typed arguments
items.text: Use clear descriptions and typed arguments as a lens for understanding designing reliable tools. Trace its inputs, the operation or decision it describes, the result a learner can observe, and the limitations that matter for the intended task. Confirm the idea with a small example and an explicit check rather than relying on fluent or plausible output.

items.title: Input validation and output normalization
items.text: Input validation and output normalization addresses how information is prepared, described, versioned, or governed. Validate the input, keep source and access metadata, handle duplicates and missing values deliberately, and test the downstream effect of a data change rather than treating the data pipeline as invisible plumbing.

items.title: Permissions and resource restrictions
items.text: Permissions and resource restrictions is a control problem as much as a model-behavior problem. Establish explicit boundaries in trusted application code, minimize data exposure, test realistic misuse and failure cases, and record who is responsible for reviewing residual risk. A prompt alone is not a security boundary.

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet and fixed sample inputs, rerun it, then change one input at a time and compare the new output with the stated contract.

content_blocks.title: Provider and version note
content_blocks.text: Model names, API payloads, supported modalities, quotas, pricing, and SDK behavior vary by provider and change over time. Treat linked official documentation as the authority for a live integration; examples here avoid hard-coded production model IDs and secrets.

content.task: Practice single-purpose tool design within designing reliable tools: use a small synthetic input, predict the result, run the example, then change one input to test an edge case. Record the expected result and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example uses a clearly described, non-sensitive input.
Expected behavior and at least one edge/failure case are written down.
The learner checks the result against an explicit criterion and records limitations.
hints: Begin with a tiny input whose expected behavior you can explain before running it.
Change one variable at a time and retain a fixed baseline for comparison.
When a model or external service is involved, inspect evidence and errors; do not treat the model response as a trusted instruction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent or plausible output is necessarily correct.
common_mistakes.fix: Use evidence, schema checks, representative test cases, and human review for consequential results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing several inputs or parameters at once.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a baseline and vary one factor at a time so the effect can be interpreted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting secrets or private source material in prompts, logs, or a public example.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic data, server-side secret storage, data minimization, and reviewed retention rules.

summary: Designing Reliable Tools is one part of a larger generative AI application lifecycle.
Use explicit inputs, criteria, and reproducible examples to test the concept.
Document uncertainty, failure modes, security considerations, and version assumptions.
